title: Rethinking Strategic Stability with China: From Coercion to Constructivism
gist: Retired Air Force nuclear officer Nicole Klingensmith argues US coercive arms-control diplomacy with China has failed because it ignores China's 'status deficit'; China expands its nuclear arsenal partly to gain recognition as an equal great power. She proposes a status-informed approach ahead of a third Trump-Xi summit: treat China as a peer, demand it table concrete proposals, and start with new areas such as AI, space, cyber or undersea rather than weapons counting.

themes.theme: Status deficit as driver of Chinese behavior

insights.claim: Status recognition, a state's position and identity as reciprocated by other states, is an untested lever in U.S.-China arms control and explains China's resistance to existing arms-control frameworks.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Suggests US-China strategic dialogue could shift if Washington changes framing, a potential de-escalation catalyst to monitor.
insights.locator: Every administration since the Cold War

insights.claim: Under social identity theory, a state with a status deficit engages in emulation, competition or creativity to gain recognition, and China's dissatisfaction with its rank and its comparison to the United States indicate such a deficit.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Framework predicts continued Chinese military emulation of the US until status is recognized, implying persistent arms competition.

insights.claim: China expands its military and nuclear capabilities to emulate and compete with the United States because they are status symbols that generate deference, and it will not give up those tools preemptively in response to U.S. demands.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Expect continued Chinese nuclear buildup absent a new framework, supporting long-run US and allied defense spending.
insights.quote: China will not accept America’s demands that it preemptively give up the very tools it perceives as critical
insights.locator: China is using its expanding military

insights.claim: The author argues that, like Putin's truthful 2007 signals, Xi has for years openly signaled China's intent to regain its 'rightful' place, including at the 20th Party Congress in 2022 and the BRICS summit on September 13, 2026, and is now demanding equality and deference.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Taking Xi's stated intentions at face value implies a structurally assertive China and elevated geopolitical risk.
insights.locator: Just as the West summarily dismissed Putin

themes.theme: Signals from the 2026 summits and dialogues

insights.claim: China's readout from the May 2026 U.S.-China summit framed 'building a constructive relationship of strategic stability' as a 'new vision', language the author reads as revealing China does not yet see itself as an equal partner.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Parsing Chinese readouts for status language can signal Beijing's negotiating stance ahead of summits.
insights.quote: If Xi believed China was already an equal partner with the United States, then the readout would reinforce the relationship as it exists

insights.claim: At a 2023 P5 meeting the author observed that China refused to join any agreement, institution or treaty it did not help create, while U.S. proposals were exactly what China said would be inappropriate, leaving both sides entrenched.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Legacy-format arms-control proposals are unlikely to succeed; expect stalemate unless the format changes.
insights.quote: China would never submit to joining anything it did not help to create
insights.locator: My own experience at a 2023 P5 meeting

insights.claim: In June 2026 Track 1.5 dialogues China still said it was not fair, reasonable or realistic to join trilateral nuclear disarmament talks, and asked the United States to keep refraining from responding to China's nuclear expansion.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: No near-term trilateral arms control means continued nuclear modernization spending in the US.
insights.quote: it is not fair, reasonable, or realistic to ask China to participate at this stage in a so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiation

insights.claim: Trump's statements after the May 2026 summit calling China one of the two 'most important and most powerful countries in the world' are, in the author's view, an early incremental step of status accommodation rather than a failure, despite criticism that he came away with little.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Status-affirming rhetoric from Trump may precede thaw in US-China relations; watch for concrete follow-through at the next summit.
insights.locator: After rolling out the red carpet

insights.claim: China appears to be offering a specific three-year timeframe to negotiate on strategic stability, with a third U.S.-China summit between Trump and Xi approaching.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: A defined negotiating window and an upcoming summit are catalysts for US-China relations and risk sentiment.

insights.claim: The author recommends the United States lead in accommodating China's status, treating it as a peer, while openly demanding China contribute concrete proposals commensurate with great-power status.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: A shift to peer-based US-China dialogue would reduce tail risk of nuclear arms racing.
insights.quote: If China wants to be treated as an equal, then the United States is right to demand that China come to the table with new, concrete proposals
insights.locator: Next, the United States should openly demand

insights.claim: Negotiations should drop the legacy 'arms control' label, set aside Taiwan, and start with new areas such as artificial intelligence, space, cyber or undersea activities, deferring capability limits and weapons counting until a new framework exists.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: US-China cooperation on AI or space governance could be a first visible deliverable affecting tech policy.
insights.quote: Negotiations should refrain from opening discussions with capability limitations or weapons counting
insights.locator: Setting aside the intractable Taiwan issue

insights.claim: If China's nuclear expansion is a path toward equality as it says, China should be pressed to reconcile its nuclear breakout and AI activities with its promises of 'peaceful development' and never engaging in an arms race.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Highlights an inconsistency the US can use diplomatically; the outcome affects nuclear and AI arms-race trajectories.
insights.quote: China cannot indefinitely have it both ways.
insights.locator: Another idea is to simply consider

insights.claim: The author argues status accommodation is a low-cost tactic that is not appeasement: if it fails, the result is simply the stagnant status quo, and the United States can keep spending on deterrence in parallel.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Low downside of the approach makes some form of it plausible policy; deterrence spending continues regardless.
insights.quote: Status recognition is a negotiation tactic of little cost compared to other bargaining tools.
insights.locator: Constructing a new form of dialogue

insights.claim: Quick political wins are unlikely; the United States should play an apolitical, impersonal long game in which success requires creativity and compromise.
insights.speaker: Nicole Klingensmith
insights.so_what: Do not expect a near-term arms-control breakthrough to change defense budgets or risk premia.
